item.text: {"chapter_id":"3B","answers":[{"question_id":"3B.1","answer":"Protection was materially inadequate and mixed. The government enacted victim-reparation and protection frameworks, adopted laws on human-rights defenders, sexual-violence reparations, trafficking, and penitentiary principles, and reported some prosecutions and releases, including Diongo’s release without charge and convictions of security personnel in the Goma case (BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0011-E002; BATCH-0003-E007; BATCH-0011-E021). However, arbitrary detention, political prosecutions, torture, disappearances, harsh prisons, and extrajudicial killings remained documented; journalists, activists, and opposition figures were detained, and security forces killed protesters in Goma and elsewhere (BATCH-0011-E008; BATCH-0010-E013; BATCH-0025-E005; BATCH-0012-R03-E002; BATCH-0025-E011; BATCH-0026-E007). Remedies were partial: investigations and trials occurred, but impunity, incomplete investigations, disputed casualty accounting, unpaid or inaccessible reparations, and weak protection persisted (BATCH-0011-E008; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0011-E021; BATCH-0028-E017; BATCH-0022-E009). The strongest adverse evidence concerns state-attributed recurring abuse, including the state-of-siege system and protest killings; some conflict killings were by armed groups and cannot be personally attributed to Tshisekedi (BATCH-0011-E009; BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0026-E012).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0003-E007","BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0029-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E002","BATCH-0011-E021","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0005-E001","BATCH-0011-E009"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Most evidence establishes government conduct rather than a personal presidential order for each incident.","National incidence, detention conditions, and remedy completion are incompletely measured.","Some grave violence was committed by non-state armed groups or occurred under contested attribution."]},{"question_id":"3B.2","answer":"Tshisekedi exercised formal command and made appointments and directives aimed at security, reform, civilian protection, and discipline, including military and judicial appointments, instructions to protect the population, military-code and training measures, and police-investigation initiatives (BATCH-0018-E005; BATCH-0019-E010; BATCH-0011-E004; BATCH-0009-E005; BATCH-0006-E001). Implementation and control were nevertheless weak. Security forces repeatedly used excessive or lethal force, journalists and protesters were beaten or detained, Mobondo fighters were transferred into military training without abuse vetting, and FARDC elements collaborated with armed groups; the government also supported or mobilized aligned forces whose conduct created accountability risks (BATCH-0026-E007; BATCH-0010-E015; BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0028-E016). Some officers were arrested, prosecuted, or convicted, but senior command accountability and nationwide prevention were not demonstrated; in the Goma case, the regional commander allegedly praised the operation and failed to ensure effective investigation (BATCH-0002-E012; BATCH-0011-E021; BATCH-0011-E022). Attribution is strongest for the state-of-siege structure, appointments, and national security strategy, but not for every local or battlefield abuse.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0019-E010","BATCH-0011-E004","BATCH-0009-E005","BATCH-0006-E001"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E012","BATCH-0011-E021","BATCH-0011-E022","BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0028-E016"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Evidence of presidential operational control over individual units and incidents is incomplete.","Official claims of training, commitments, and reduced abuse are largely self-reported or not independently quantified.","Aligned-actor and regional-force conduct cannot uniformly be attributed to the president."]},{"question_id":"3B.3","answer":"The record is mixed but adverse on the operational environment. Tshisekedi sometimes used unifying language, called for love, unity, equality, and rejection of divisiveness, and the state retained formal prohibitions on ethnic and xenophobic hate speech (BATCH-0020-E015; BATCH-0016-E003). Conversely, he publicly threatened people deemed threats to national security, stated he would act without hesitation or regret despite human-rights criticism, warned against allegedly foreign-manufactured candidates, and used highly adversarial rhetoric against Rwanda and M23; the latter was primarily external-conflict rhetoric, not necessarily domestic incitement (BATCH-0003-E010; BATCH-0018-E007; BATCH-0007-E013; BATCH-0009-E009). Ruling-party or aligned officials and supporters were implicated in ethnic-regional incitement, attacks on journalists, sexual violence, and political violence; the evidence rarely shows Tshisekedi authored or endorsed those messages, but it also rarely shows effective discipline after notice (BATCH-0002-E014; BATCH-0002-E017; BATCH-0006-E004; BATCH-0027-E002; BATCH-0027-E005). Hate speech and interethnic hostility increased during the campaign, with weak provincial regulation and incomplete accountability (BATCH-0001-E014; BATCH-0006-E009; BATCH-0010-E021).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E015","BATCH-0016-E003"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E010","BATCH-0018-E007","BATCH-0002-E017","BATCH-0006-E004","BATCH-0010-E021","BATCH-0007-E013"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Direct presidential incitement against domestic protected groups is not clearly established.","Many harmful acts were committed by supporters or officials without proven presidential authorization.","The effects of presidential rhetoric on subsequent violence are not causally demonstrated."]},{"question_id":"3B.4","answer":"Oversight and remedy existed but were not reliably independent or effective. Positive measures included the 2023 ICC cooperation agreement and investigation request, recruitment and training of magistrates, mobile courts, selected convictions, a victim-reparations framework, a national reparations fund, a National Commission on Human Rights, and some police and judicial investigations (BATCH-0019-E001; BATCH-0019-E002; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0011-E014). Adverse evidence shows judicial interference, politically manipulated courts, denied access to military and intelligence detention sites, scarce resources, unpaid reparations, stalled investigations, and prosecutions lacking individualized evidence (BATCH-0011-E008; BATCH-0011-E014; BATCH-0028-E017; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0011-E021). The Goma killings illustrate the gap between formal investigation and effective remedy: bodies were not properly identified, ballistic or autopsy work was absent, civilian prosecutions were criticized, and accountability remained incomplete despite some convictions (BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0011-E021). Tshisekedi’s judicial appointments and reshuffles demonstrate authority over personnel, but their independence and corrective effect are not established (BATCH-0015-E006; BATCH-0019-E005; BATCH-0019-E006).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0019-E002","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0011-E014"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E008","BATCH-0011-E020","BATCH-0011-E021","BATCH-0028-E017","BATCH-0015-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Institutional independence is difficult to infer from formal appointments alone.","Many reported investigations lack final findings or verified victim compensation.","Some accountability activity was supported by UN or international actors, limiting presidential attribution."]},{"question_id":"3B.5","answer":"Exceptional security powers were used broadly and only partly reviewed or narrowed. Tshisekedi maintained and repeatedly extended the state of siege more than 50 times, transferred civilian administration to military and police authorities, subjected civilians to military courts, and failed to provide the required international derogation notification according to Amnesty (BATCH-0012-R03-E001; BATCH-0012-R03-E003; BATCH-0012-R03-E007). The regime coincided with arbitrary detention, harassment of critics, restrictions on assembly and expression, and worsening civilian insecurity (BATCH-0012-R03-E002; BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0009-E002). A potentially favorable corrective step was the August national roundtable to consider maintaining, requalifying, or lifting the regime, followed by an October announcement of gradual easing, including ending a curfew and allowing demonstrations; the supplied evidence does not establish full implementation or reversal of abuses by year-end (BATCH-0007-E002; BATCH-0021-E012; BATCH-0008-E007). Surveillance and anti-terror provisions also enabled journalist and critic prosecutions, while the revised press law retained prison exposure for press offenses (BATCH-0025-E007; BATCH-0025-E011; BATCH-0025-E012).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R03-E001","BATCH-0012-R03-E003","BATCH-0009-E002","BATCH-0015-E007"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0007-E002","BATCH-0021-E012","BATCH-0008-E007","BATCH-0025-E007"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The complete legal text, legislative review, and geographic scope of each extension are not supplied.","The evidence does not establish the precise presidential role in every detention or prosecution.","The counterfactual security effect of the state of siege cannot be measured confidently."]},{"question_id":"3B.6","answer":"Domestic safety outcomes were poor and mixed. Documented violations decreased 12% from 2022 to 2023, and some ceasefire agreements temporarily reduced hostilities, but conflict-related killings, displacement, sexual violence, and armed-group activity remained extensive (BATCH-0025-E009; BATCH-0027-E006). More than 1,480 civilians were victims of summary or extrajudicial killings in the first half of 2023, more than 100 armed groups remained active, ADF attacks caused over 1,000 reported fatalities, and violence rose around the election period (BATCH-0011-E009; BATCH-0010-E015; BATCH-0027-E007; BATCH-0026-E012). The state-of-siege strategy failed to curb widespread violence and was associated with serious state abuses, including the Goma protest killings, so any security effort cannot be treated as a lawful safety gain without qualification (BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0011-E018). Government and regional operations, MONUSCO cooperation, ceasefire diplomacy, and planned disarmament were plausible protective measures, but outcomes were limited or reversed when agreements broke down and M23 expanded (BATCH-0011-E010; BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0016-E005; BATCH-0027-E006). Most conflict deaths were caused by non-state actors or multiple parties, constraining direct presidential causation.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0025-E009","BATCH-0011-E010","BATCH-0016-E005","BATCH-0021-E001"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E009","BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0027-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Reported violations are incomplete and affected by access, fear, and changing reporting conditions.","No reliable exposure-adjusted national crime or violence counterfactual is provided.","External armed groups, regional intervention, and conflict geography materially constrain attribution."]},{"question_id":"3B.7","answer":"Protection of vulnerable groups was formally expanded but substantively inadequate. The government enacted Indigenous-peoples protections, sexual-violence and victim-reparation laws, child-protection measures, gender-violence services, mobile clinics, safe spaces, and programs for displaced children and survivors (BATCH-0001-E010; BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0011-E006; BATCH-0010-E006; BATCH-0029-E006). There were some service outputs, including assistance to survivors, maternal care, child reunification, and support for women’s socioeconomic integration, but much of this was delivered by UN or partner agencies rather than the presidency (BATCH-0002-E010; BATCH-0025-E003; BATCH-0016-E017; BATCH-0011-E006). Adverse outcomes were severe: displacement reached roughly 6.8–6.9 million, women and girls faced heightened rape and assault risks, sexual violence increased, children were recruited, and access to health, protection, compensation, and camps was limited (BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0008-E003; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0010-E002; BATCH-0022-E012). Forced evictions, mining-related violence, discrimination, and regional access gaps further weakened equitable protection (BATCH-0010-E018; BATCH-0002-E022; BATCH-0013-E016).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0011-E006","BATCH-0010-E006","BATCH-0001-E010","BATCH-0029-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E010","BATCH-0025-E003","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0008-E003","BATCH-0010-E018","BATCH-0002-E022"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Government funding, coverage, and enforcement are often not separated from donor and humanitarian contributions.","Many outcome figures are regional, estimated, or not specific to state perpetrators.","Equity across provinces and protected groups is insufficiently measured."]},{"question_id":"3B.8","answer":"Peaceful protest, dissent, and journalism were not reliably protected. Formal commitments and some corrective actions existed, including a 2023 electoral-security directive, arrests of three officers after the May march, the announced easing of the state of siege, and occasional peaceful police escort of demonstrations (BATCH-0009-E001; BATCH-0002-E012; BATCH-0008-E007; BATCH-0022-E014). In practice, authorities blocked or banned opposition gatherings, used tear gas and beatings, detained journalists and critics, and repeatedly restricted political movement; the May march caused serious injuries, while the August Goma operation killed dozens and detained scores (BATCH-0003-E002; BATCH-0003-E003; BATCH-0003-E004; BATCH-0011-E011; BATCH-0011-E018). Journalists faced arbitrary arrests, threats, attacks, disappearances, and prosecutions, including the detention of Bujakera and attacks by ruling-party supporters (BATCH-0025-E008; BATCH-0025-E012; BATCH-0027-E002). Some officers were detained or investigated, but remedies were incomplete and command responsibility was not established; direct presidential attribution is strongest for public praise of the police chief and the broader security framework, not every local incident (BATCH-0002-E011; BATCH-0011-E022).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-E001","BATCH-0002-E012","BATCH-0022-E014"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E004","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0011-E011","BATCH-0025-E012","BATCH-0027-E002","BATCH-0002-E011"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Some protests were formally unauthorized and the legality or proportionality of particular restrictions is unresolved.","Casualty figures for Goma are disputed.","Many attacks were committed by party supporters or local officials without proven presidential orders."]},{"question_id":"3B.9","answer":"Crisis response combined protective planning with militarization, delayed correction, and serious civilian harm. The government convened security and crisis meetings, pursued ceasefire and disarmament arrangements, planned MONUSCO transition, deployed forces in some communal crises, created patrols, and announced humanitarian and protective programs (BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0005-E005; BATCH-0018-E001; BATCH-0010-E007; BATCH-0011-E003). However, responses to Kwamouth violence were delayed and assistance to displaced people was inadequate; eastern conflict displacement and humanitarian need continued to rise; and the state-of-siege and Goma operations used military force against civilians, including lethal suppression of a banned protest (BATCH-0011-E001; BATCH-003?; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0011-E019). The president’s rhetoric emphasized security, military victory, recruitment, and resistance to M23, while dialogue and ceasefire implementation repeatedly failed or were narrowed by hardline positions (BATCH-0007-E013; BATCH-0011-E017; BATCH-0027-E006). Some post-incident investigations and prosecutions were announced, but their independence, completeness, and corrective effect remain uncertain (BATCH-0023-E014; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0011-E021).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0018-E001","BATCH-0010-E007","BATCH-0011-E003"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E001","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0011-E019","BATCH-0007-E013","BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0023-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The candidate index lacks a complete national crisis-budget allocation and execution record.","Some cited humanitarian responses were led by international agencies, not the government.","One referenced ID is unavailable in the supplied index and should not be relied upon."]},{"question_id":"3B.10","answer":"The evidence does not show that people were durably safer by the end of 2023. There were limited favorable indicators: documented human-rights violations fell 12% year-on-year, some ceasefires temporarily reduced hostilities, certain legal and justice capacities expanded, and the government cooperated with ICC, UN, and regional processes (BATCH-0025-E009; BATCH-0027-E006; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0019-E001). Against that, national displacement reached approximately 6.8–6.9 million, eastern violence and armed-group control persisted or worsened, ADF and M23 violence remained high, and the state-of-siege policy failed to deliver its stated protection objective while enabling state abuses (BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0027-E007; BATCH-0012-R03-E004). State-attributed repression, arbitrary detention, protest killings, journalist persecution, and weak remedy meant that non-state violence was not replaced by dependable lawful protection (BATCH-0011-E008; BATCH-0011-E011; BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0028-E015). The comparison is constrained by inherited conflict, regional intervention, armed-group responsibility, population exposure, and underreporting; therefore the adverse end-state is clear, but the precise share caused by Tshisekedi rather than external shocks is uncertain.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0025-E009","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0021-E007"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0028-E015","BATCH-0027-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No complete exposure-adjusted baseline or counterfactual for 2019–2023 is supplied.","Reported violence is affected by access, censorship, conflict geography, and humanitarian reporting capacity.","Presidential authority over non-state and foreign actors was limited, while state-force attribution is clearer than total-conflict attribution."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["The dominant pattern is recurring and widespread insecurity with significant state-attributed repression, but not evidence in the supplied index of a nationwide mass-terror system.","Formal laws, appointments, investigations, and international cooperation coexisted with weak implementation, impunity, militarized emergency governance, and incomplete remedy.","The strongest direct presidential attribution concerns maintaining the state of siege, appointing and directing security institutions, publicly praising or defending security responses, and setting hardline crisis rhetoric; attribution for individual local abuses and armed-group violence is often indirect or uncertain.","Open reporting provides substantial evidence of abuse, while conflict zones and closed security institutions likely produce undercounting; lower documented violations therefore cannot be treated as equivalent to broad safety improvement.","Humanitarian and UN programs generated protective outputs, but their funding and implementation were frequently external or shared, limiting credit to Tshisekedi personally."]}
